title: DOES “LUST” SETTLE THE MASTURBATION QUESTION—or Is the Biblical Discussion More Complicated?
paragraphs: DOES “LUST” SETTLE THE MASTURBATION QUESTION—or Is the Biblical Discussion More Complicated?

Jesus spoke directly about lust. Paul spoke about sexual holiness, self-mastery, conscience, and glorifying God with the body. But the Bible never actually uses the word “masturbation.” So what happens when we stop repeating slogans, open the Scriptures, and allow the text to ask harder questions than the ones we expected?
There are sins people confess at the altar.
And then there are sins—or struggles, questions, habits, wounds, compulsions—that people carry home.
Quietly.
They worship on Sunday.
They raise their hands.
They quote Scripture.
They love Jesus.
Then midnight comes.
The bedroom door closes.
The phone lights up.
The loneliness gets louder.
The body remembers what the conscience has been trying to forget.
And afterward?
Silence.
Sometimes shame.
Sometimes repentance.
Sometimes confusion.
Sometimes the exhausted prayer of a Christian who has promised God for the fiftieth time, “Lord, I will never do this again.”
And sometimes there is another question—one many believers are almost afraid to ask because they assume merely asking it makes them rebellious:
What, precisely, does the Bible actually say about masturbation?
Not what Christian culture says.
Not what pornography says.
Not what secular culture says.
Not what your guilt says.
Not what somebody’s viral video says.
What does Scripture say?
Because there is a dangerous way to become “biblical” that actually requires putting words into the Bible that the Bible never says.
And there is an equally dangerous way to exploit biblical silence as permission to indulge whatever the flesh desires.
Neither is faithful.
So stay with me.
Because this discussion becomes much more uncomfortable before it becomes hopeful.
And somewhere underneath the question about masturbation may be another question entirely:
Who owns your body when nobody else is watching?
Jesus gives us one of the most important texts in this conversation in Matthew 5:28.
The Greek reads:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
A close rendering is:
“But I say to you that everyone looking at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Pay attention to the expression:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai
The verb epithymeō can mean to desire, long for, covet, or—depending upon context—lust.
And the construction here matters.
Jesus is not teaching that noticing that another human being is physically attractive is automatically adultery.
He is going after something deeper.
The look that becomes intentional desire.
The gaze that welcomes and cultivates sexual possession in the heart.
The human being standing before you—or appearing on your screen—ceases to be treated as someone bearing God's image and becomes material for your imagination.
Jesus moves the courtroom into the heart.
That changes this entire discussion.

Because if masturbation is being fueled by pornography, deliberately cultivated fantasies about someone who is not your spouse, voyeurism, sexually exploitative imagery, or intentional fantasizing designed to produce lust, then we cannot simply isolate the physical act from what the heart is doing.
The question is no longer merely:
“Did my body experience sexual release?”
The question becomes:
What did I ask my heart to consume in order to get there?
That is harder.
Because nobody else may have been in the room.
But someone may have been in your imagination.
Someone whose body became raw material for your gratification.
Someone who never consented to occupy the sexual world you constructed inside your mind.
And Jesus cares about what happens there.
Not because sexual desire itself is dirty.

God created human beings as embodied creatures. Scripture does not teach that possessing sexual desire makes you filthy. The biblical story affirms marriage, one-flesh union, marital intimacy, desire, embodiment, and the goodness of God's creation.
The problem is not that you possess a body.
The problem is what sin can teach us to do with desire.
Paul puts the matter this way in 1 Thessalonians 4:3:
Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας.
“This is the will of God—your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
The word ἁγιασμός — hagiasmos speaks of holiness or sanctification.
And πορνεία — porneia refers broadly to sexual immorality.
A few verses later Paul speaks of not living:
ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας — en pathei epithymias
“In passion of lust/desire.”
So yes.
Lust matters enormously.
But here is where Christians must resist saying more than Scripture says.
The Bible never directly names masturbation as an act.
There is no verse that says, “You shall not masturbate.”
That fact should neither frighten us nor become a loophole.
It should make us more careful interpreters.
Some people immediately run to Onan.

Genesis 38 tells how Judah commanded Onan to fulfill his obligation toward his deceased brother's wife and raise offspring for his brother. The Hebrew text speaks of raising זֶרַע — zeraʿ, “seed” or offspring, for his brother.
Onan understood that the offspring would not be reckoned as his.
So during intercourse with his brother's widow, he deliberately prevented conception rather than fulfilling the obligation placed upon him.
Genesis says what he did was wicked before the LORD.
But read the story carefully.
The text describes intercourse and Onan's deliberate refusal to provide offspring for his deceased brother.
It does not describe masturbation.

Whatever broader ethical conclusions Christians may draw from the passage, turning Genesis 38 into a straightforward verse saying “God killed Onan for masturbating” does not accurately represent what the narrative actually says.
And Christians should never need a distorted Bible verse to defend holiness.
Truth does not need our exaggeration.
But now someone may say:
“Then masturbation must be okay.”
Not so fast.
Biblical ethics often works through more than a dictionary of explicitly named behaviors.
Paul gives us a devastating principle in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει... ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.
“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial... I will not be mastered by anything.”
That final idea deserves to sit in the room with us for a moment.
I will not be mastered by anything.
Because perhaps the question you have been asking is:
“Can I do it?”
When another question may expose much more:
“Can I stop?”
That changes things.
Can you walk away for a week?
A month?
Can you sleep without it?
Can you experience stress without running toward it?
Can you feel lonely without immediately needing sexual release?
Can you encounter temptation without opening pornography?
Can you pray when the urge comes instead of automatically obeying it?
Can you say no?
Or has what you once called relief slowly become a master?
There is an enormous difference between having an appetite and being ruled by one.
Paul does not merely ask whether something appears on a forbidden-behavior list.
He asks whether it is beneficial.
Whether it dominates.
Whether it belongs with holiness.
Whether the body is being offered to God.
Then Paul says something staggering:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς· δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.
“You were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
Perhaps the deepest question in the entire discussion.
Not merely:
“Is masturbation technically forbidden?”
But:
“Can I bring this before Jesus without hiding?”
Can I thank Him for it?
Can I practice it in faith?
Can I say, “Lord Jesus, this body belongs to You. Be glorified in what I am about to do”?
Can I do it without pornography?
Without mentally possessing another person?
Without feeding fantasies that violate Christ's teaching about the heart?
Without being mastered?
Without violating my conscience?
Without using sexual pleasure as anesthesia for wounds Jesus is asking me to bring into His light?
Those questions do not manufacture a commandment Scripture never gives.
They do something much more searching.
They bring the behavior underneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that may expose another uncomfortable truth.
For some people, masturbation is not primarily a sexual problem.
It has become pain medication.
You are lonely.
You do it.
Rejected.
You do it.
Anxious.
You do it.
Depressed.
You do it.
Angry with your spouse.
You do it.
Feeling unwanted.
You do it.
Unable to sleep.
You do it.
Ashamed that you did it yesterday.
And somehow...
you do it again.
The body becomes the place where an emotional wound repeatedly demands anesthesia.
And this is where shouting “STOP LUSTING!” may fail to reach the actual battlefield.
Yes, sinful lust must be resisted.
Yes, pornography must be rejected.
Yes, sexual immorality must be fled.
But sometimes discipleship must also ask:
What are you trying not to feel?
What loneliness keeps returning?
What rejection are you medicating?
What wound keeps asking for relief?
What happened to you?
What are you afraid to tell anyone?
Why does darkness feel safer than being known?
This does not excuse sin.
It helps expose where the battle is actually being fought.
Because Jesus does not merely want to take pornography out of your browser history.
He wants your heart.
He does not merely want cleaner behavior.
He wants freedom.
Paul writes in Galatians 5:16:
Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς οὐ μὴ τελέσητε.
“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desire of the flesh.”
Notice the direction.
Walk by the Spirit.
Christian holiness is not merely spending the rest of your life screaming “NO!” at your body.
It is learning to say a greater “YES” to Christ.
Yes to prayer.
Yes to truth.
Yes to bringing temptation into the light.
Yes to accountability.
Yes to removing pornography rather than negotiating with it.
Yes to getting the phone out of the bedroom if that phone repeatedly becomes a doorway.
Yes to calling a mature Christian when secrecy begins whispering again.
Yes to learning how to suffer loneliness without worshiping relief.
Yes to learning that an urge can exist without becoming your master.
And yes—even after failure—to getting up again.
Somebody reading this failed last night.
Maybe this morning.
Maybe five minutes before finding this article.
And you almost stopped reading because every paragraph felt like someone opening curtains in a room you desperately wanted dark.
Listen carefully.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Shame says:
“Hide until you become worthy of the light.”
Those voices are not saying the same thing.
The Gospel does not tell sinners to cleanse themselves enough to approach Jesus.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The cross is not God's declaration that your sin does not matter.
The cross is the terrifying proof that sin matters more than we imagined—and the breathtaking proof that God's grace reaches farther than we deserved.
“If we confess our sins,” Scripture says, “He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Do not confuse no condemnation with no transformation.
Grace does not say:
“Stay chained.”
Grace walks into the prison carrying keys.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely so you could become more comfortable hiding.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confessing.
Delete what needs deleting.
Block what needs blocking.
Bring into community what secrecy has protected.
If pornography is involved, stop pretending the masturbation question can be separated from pornography.
If deliberate lustful fantasy is involved, bring the fantasy under Matthew 5:28.
If the behavior controls you, bring it under Paul's refusal to “be mastered by anything.”
If your conscience is continually accusing you, do not repeatedly bulldoze your conscience merely because you found somebody online willing to give you permission.

And if your struggle has become compulsive, entrenched, or connected to trauma, loneliness, anxiety, or other deep wounds, seeking help from a trustworthy pastor, mature Christian mentor, or qualified professional is not spiritual defeat.
Sometimes walking into the light sounds like:
“I need help.”
Perhaps you have spent years asking God:
“Why can't I stop?”
Maybe tonight the prayer needs to change.
“Jesus, show me what I have been running from.”
That prayer can become frightening.
Because He may show you the pornography.
The fantasy.
The loneliness.
The resentment.
The boredom.
The secret entitlement.
The unhealed rejection.
The habit.
The self-pity.
The craving for control.
Maybe even the religious shame that convinced you God was disgusted every time you stumbled and therefore made you hide from the only One who could heal you.
Bring all of it.
Not just the respectable pieces.
Bring the scandal.
That is what grace is for.
And no, this article cannot honestly reduce every circumstance to the simplistic sentence, “Masturbation equals lust, therefore the discussion is over.”
Scripture deserves better than that.
Neither can we say, “The Bible doesn't mention the word, therefore anything goes.”
Scripture deserves better than that too.
The faithful question reaches deeper.
What accompanies the act?
What feeds it?
What does the heart intentionally desire?
Does pornography participate?
Does another person become an object inside the imagination?
Does it strengthen self-control or weaken it?
Is it mastering you?
Can it be brought honestly before Christ?
Does it move you toward holiness or repeatedly into secrecy?
Can you genuinely seek to glorify God in your body while doing it?
Those questions may produce different pastoral complexities, but they refuse both legalistic invention and convenient loopholes.
And perhaps that is why this subject hurts.
Because eventually it stops being about winning an argument concerning masturbation.
It becomes about surrender.
Jesus does not want one sanitized corner of you.
He wants you.
Your sexuality.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your browser history.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your body.
Your desires.
Your failures.
Your future.
All of you.
And the hands of Christ are not the hands of a disgusted Savior reluctantly touching contaminated people.
Those hands were pierced.
For sinners.
For the ashamed.
For people with histories they wish they could erase.
For people who promised “never again” and then did it again.
For people who have become experts at worshiping publicly while bleeding privately.
The Gospel is not that you finally became strong enough to save yourself.
The Gospel is that Christ came when you could not.
Died for sinners.
Rose victorious.
Calls us to repentance.
Forgives those who come to Him.
And begins making His people new.
So if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to write the details publicly.
But you can stop pretending.

And please remember: the comment section should never become a confessional booth for graphic details. Protect your privacy. Protect others. Confess specific sins to God and, where appropriate, to trustworthy people who can actually walk with you.

If someone came into your mind while reading this—someone fighting pornography, shame, secret sexual habits, loneliness, or the exhausting cycle of falling and hiding—send this article to them privately.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that there is still a door out of darkness.
It does not.
Only Jesus saves.
Christian giving is meant to come willingly from the heart, not through spiritual coercion.
Pray.
Share.
Save the teachings that help you.
Support the spread of biblical truth in whatever faithful way God enables you.
Because ultimately this ministry is not about building an audience around Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing an audience beyond Gospel Warrior...
to Jesus.
The One who sees what happens after the bedroom door closes.
The One who knows what nobody else knows.
The One who refuses to call darkness light.
And the One whose grace is powerful enough that your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
You may be ashamed of the chapter you wrote in secret—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still capable of writing redemption across the page.
